lessons.title: The accounting equation and the three statements

scenes.text: Kavya puts ₹5,00,000 of her savings into a new design studio and opens a business bank account.
She buys equipment for ₹2,00,000 cash and takes a ₹1,00,000 bank loan for working capital.
Her accountant says: whatever happens, assets will always equal liabilities plus owner's equity.

steps.title: Assets = Liabilities + Equity
steps.body:
**Assets** are resources the firm controls (cash, receivables, inventory, equipment). **Liabilities** are obligations to outsiders (loans, payables). **Equity** is the owners' residual claim.

Every transaction changes at least two items so the equation always balances - this is double-entry bookkeeping.

The three statements: the **balance sheet** (position at a date), the **income statement** (performance over a period) and the **cash flow statement** (cash movements over a period).

steps.title: Solved example · Kavya's balance sheet
steps.body:
- Start: cash 5,00,000 = equity 5,00,000.
- Buy equipment 2,00,000 cash: cash 3,00,000, equipment 2,00,000.
- Loan 1,00,000: cash 4,00,000, loan (liability) 1,00,000.

Total assets = 4,00,000 + 2,00,000 = **6,00,000**. Liabilities 1,00,000 + equity 5,00,000 = **6,00,000**. Balanced.

Next she earns ₹80,000 service revenue in cash and pays ₹50,000 expenses in cash: profit ₹30,000 raises equity to **₹5,30,000**.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Treating a loan received as income - it is a liability, not revenue.
- Treating owner's drawings as an expense - they reduce equity directly.
- Forgetting that revenue is recognised when earned, not necessarily when cash arrives (accrual basis).

scenes.text: Sundaram Components applies for a working-capital limit and sends its year-end statements to the bank.

steps.title: The core ratio families
steps.body:
- **Liquidity:** Current ratio = CA / CL; Quick ratio = (CA − Inventory) / CL.
- **Profitability:** Net margin = Net profit / Sales; ROE = Net profit / Equity.
- **Leverage:** Debt-equity = Debt / Equity; Interest cover = EBIT / Interest.
- **Efficiency:** Inventory turnover = COGS / Average inventory.

steps.title: Solved example
steps.body:
Sundaram: current assets ₹6,00,000 (inventory ₹2,00,000), current liabilities ₹3,00,000, sales ₹12,00,000, net profit ₹1,20,000, debt ₹8,00,000, equity ₹4,00,000.

- Current ratio = 6/3 = **2.0**
- Quick ratio = (6 − 2)/3 = **1.33**
- Net margin = 1.2/12 = **10%**
- ROE = 1.2/4 = **30%**
- Debt-equity = 8/4 = **2.0**

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Using closing instead of average balances for turnover ratios without saying so.
- Comparing ratios across industries - a current ratio of 1.0 is fine for a retailer, risky for a project contractor.
- Reading ROE alone: high ROE can come from heavy debt, not good operations.

steps.title: Indirect method
steps.body:
Start with net profit. Add back non-cash expenses (depreciation). Subtract increases in current assets (receivables, inventory). Add increases in operating current liabilities (payables).

The statement has three sections: operating, investing and financing.

- Putting interest paid and dividends in the wrong section; treat each policy consistently.

steps.title: The EOQ formula
steps.body: **EOQ = √(2DS/H)**, where D = annual demand, S = cost per order and H = holding cost per unit per year. Total annual cost = (D/Q)·S + (Q/2)·H, and at the EOQ the ordering cost equals the holding cost.

steps.title: Solved example
steps.body:
- EOQ = √(2 × 1,200 × 50 / 3) = √40,000 = **200 bottles**
- Orders a year = 1,200/200 = 6 → ordering cost ₹300
- Average stock = 100 → holding cost ₹300
- Total relevant cost = **₹600** a year.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Using monthly demand with an annual holding cost.
- Forgetting that H is often given as a % of the unit price (e.g. 20% of ₹15 = ₹3).
- Treating EOQ as exact: the cost curve is flat near the optimum, so round sensibly.

steps.title: Core formulas
steps.body:
Future value: **FV = PV × (1+r)^n**. Present value: **PV = FV / (1+r)^n**. Discount rate r reflects opportunity cost and risk.

An ordinary annuity (payments at period end) has **PV = C × [1 − (1+r)^−n] / r**.

steps.title: Worked example
steps.body: ₹1,00,000 at 7% for 1 year → ₹1,07,000. The ₹1,08,000 offer is better by ₹1,000 in year-1 money, if risk is equal.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: Mixing a monthly rate with annual periods; using nominal rate for compounding without dividing by m; forgetting annuity-due (start of period) needs ×(1+r).

steps.title: Effective annual rate
steps.body: EAR = (1 + APR/m)^m − 1. A 12% nominal rate compounded monthly has EAR ≈ 12.68%.

steps.body: EMI = P × r × (1+r)^n / [(1+r)^n − 1], with r = annual rate/12 and n = months.

steps.title: Time-series forecasting
steps.body: A time-series method assumes that the future resembles the past pattern: level, trend, seasonality and noise. The **n-period moving average** forecasts F(t+1) = average of the last n actuals. It lags behind trends and treats all n points equally.

steps.title: Exponential smoothing
steps.body: F(t+1) = F(t) + α·(A(t) − F(t)). With α = 0.2, previous forecast 125 and actual 140: F = 125 + 0.2×15 = **128**. High α reacts fast but is noisy; low α is smooth but slow.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Using moving average on a strongly trending series (it always lags).
- Choosing α by taste instead of testing which α minimises error on history.
- Forgetting that the first forecast needs an initial value.

Let's work out what is really going on — step by step.

steps.title: Break-even
steps.body: Make cost = F + vQ; buy cost = pQ. Break-even Q = F/(p − v). Above that volume, making is cheaper; consider capacity, quality, IP and strategic control as well.

steps.title: Qualitative factors
steps.body: Core competence, supplier risk, lead time and capacity can outweigh a small cost gap.

activity.prompt: Break-even quantity: F=₹2,00,000, v=₹40, p=₹60.

options: variable cost is below the buy price
quiz.why: Spread fixed cost over more units.

scenes.text: Weights: cost 40%, quality 30%, delivery 20%, service 10%. Supplier A scores 8, 7, 9, 6 out of 10.
Let's work out what is really going on — step by step.

steps.title: Weighted-point method
steps.body: Score = Σ weight × rating. Weights must sum to 1 and reflect strategy. Review after delivery data arrive (on-time-in-full, PPM defects, responsiveness).

steps.title: Kraljic matrix
steps.body: Classify spend into leverage, strategic, bottleneck and non-critical to choose a sourcing stance.

scenes.text: Quote ₹100/unit + ₹5 freight; 2% of units fail inspection and each rework costs ₹50.
Let's work out what is really going on — step by step.

steps.title: TCO
steps.body: TCO = purchase price + acquisition cost (freight, duty, ordering) + usage/quality cost (rework, downtime) + disposal. A lower quote can lose on TCO.

steps.title: Compare apples to apples
steps.body: Convert all quotes into landed, quality-adjusted cost per usable unit.

scenes.text: Your incumbent supplier asks for a 6% price rise citing steel costs; a rival quotes 3% lower but untested.
Let's work out what is really going on — step by step.

steps.title: Negotiation preparation
steps.body: Know your BATNA, target and walk-away, and the supplier's costs. Trade across dimensions (volume commitment, payment terms, price indexation), not just price.

steps.title: Index clause
steps.body: Tie price to a published steel index with a collar so changes are transparent and symmetric.

steps.title: Ethics
steps.body: Never share one bidder's price with another, and avoid conflicts of interest; follow your code of conduct.

a.text: The incumbent asks for +6%. What is your best opening move?

choices.label: Ask for their cost breakdown and propose an index-linked formula plus a volume commitment
choices.feedback: Good: it tests the claim and creates a fair mechanism.

choices.label: Accept at once to avoid conflict
choices.feedback: You give away value and set a precedent.

choices.label: Switch to the unknown rival immediately
choices.feedback: Risky: untested quality and switching costs.

e.text: You secure a clause linked to the index with a cap; the rival quote becomes your fallback.
